Most failures are "unseen" cases where the correct answer never showed up within the sampling budget — these tend to be low-probability questions. The "seen" failures are trickier: shared-trap cases where a distractor scores highly across all variants, making them essentially unresolvable. Looking at the first example, truth 6173 appeared three times with weak scores while a trap consistently scored higher in one variant — a case we simply lost.

Since noise answers are random and never repeat across variants, any repeated answer string is strong evidence it's legitimate, even with a low individual score. I'm considering flooring the noise-penalty LLR for answers seen in at least two variants, since currently the repetition bonus only counts variants above the noise threshold. This seems like a rare but cheap fix — checking the data, correct answers scoring below 0.2 happen in only about 2-3% of cases across algebra and geometry, so this wouldn't move the needle much, but it's still worth patching.

I also want to trace through why this particular question at confidence 4.9 didn't reach the done threshold of 7 — the heap pops least-confident questions first, so it likely got starved of budget rather than actually converging.

More broadly, I'm looking at where sampling budget goes overall: unseen failures dominate, especially on algebra where about 10.6% of questions fail with only ~8 samples each, since a quarter of questions sit at true probability ≤0.15 and can't reliably be found within budget. Questions with zero candidates (all noise) end up with the lowest confidence scores, so the heap prioritizes sampling them up to the cap of 20 — but I'm questioning whether spending 20 samples on a question with p=0.05 is actually worth it, given how the expected marginal gain from each additional sample decays.

I'm weighing a value-of-information approach: for unseen questions, estimate p̂ using a Bayesian update from a prior (something like (0+a)/(n+b)), so the expected gain per sample is roughly the probability the next sample both succeeds and becomes the new winner. For easy topics the gain is close to p̂ itself, while for hard topics with an existing leading candidate, the gain depends on the probability the current answer is wrong times the probability a new sample flips it. The simpler fix might just be to let "no-candidate" confidence grow with n using something like p̂ ≈ 1/(n+2), so priority naturally decreases as more noise samples accumulate.

I want to test a couple of variants against the held-out set: setting unseen priority to -2 + 0.4*n, and comparing max samples per question at 16 vs 20 vs 30 — though the simulation caps out at 20 samples per question, so I'll keep it there. I'm also considering capping the hard-topic confidence measure at min(margin, e+3), and I should confirm the full 2400-sample budget gets used, which it does.

I'll build a separate priority() method distinct from confidence, and test the variants carefully across both held-out sets so I don't overfit.
